question.problem: Using the standard form of the Maclaurin series of $\frac{1}{1+x},$ find the first three non-zero terms of the series expansion of the definite integral ${\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+x}\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
The power series expansion of $\frac{1}{1+x}$ is given by 

$$
\frac{1}{1+x}=1-x+{x}^{2}-⋯.
$$

Now, we multiply the above by ${x}^{2}.$

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+x}={x}^{2}-{x}^{3}+{x}^{4}-⋯.
$$

Finally, we calculate the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{x}^{2}}{1+x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{3}+{x}^{4}-⋯)\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-⋯){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{5}-⋯\end{aligned}
$$
